context: procurement & structural-steel led · heavy-machine foundations drive the critical path; commissioning is a line-by-line ramp

brief.intro: A heavy industrial factory or process plant is a production building built around heavy machines — presses, furnaces, mixers, mills — and the material-handling systems (conveyors, cranes) that tie them into a line. Unlike a light assembly plant, the equipment here is heavy and vibration-sensitive, so it needs isolated foundations designed for load and dynamics, not just a level slab. The programme is procurement-led: heavy equipment and structural-steel packages carry long lead times and drive the critical path more than the building envelope does. Utilities — power, compressed air, cooling water, sometimes steam — must be proven before any line can be energised. Commissioning does not happen in one event; it runs line-by-line, ending in a no-load then loaded production ramp.

glossary.plain: Factory Acceptance Test at the vendor's works, then a Site Acceptance Test after the machine is installed.
first running equipment empty to prove the mechanics, then with real product to prove output.
a heavy, separate foundation block that stops a machine's vibration reaching the rest of the structure.
a piece of equipment pre-assembled off-site (e.g. a compressor or dosing unit) delivered as one lift.
safety/process logic that stops one machine unless another is in the right state — e.g. a conveyor won't run unless the downstream bin isn't full.
the software layer that tracks production and talks to the machine controllers (PLCs).
running the line at target throughput to confirm it actually hits the design production rate.

must_get_right: Sequence heavy foundations and structural steel ahead of machine delivery — machines cannot be set on unfinished floors or foundations.
Treat utility readiness (power, air, cooling) as a gating milestone before any line energisation, not a background task.
Plan commissioning line-by-line — FAT → SAT → line integration → ramp per line, staggered, not one building-wide event.
Protect a genuine no-load-to-loaded ramp window at the end — first-run issues are common and re-tests eat float.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day week; equipment set and MEP fit-out move to two shifts at peak to protect the critical path; commissioning runs a 7-day calendar once lines start FAT-to-SAT. A weather allowance is embedded in the civil calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs long-lead equipment/steel procurement → heavy foundations → structural steel → equipment set & alignment → utility termination → line integration → no-load run → loaded ramp-up. Material handling and instrumentation feed into line integration but do not usually drive the path unless procurement slips.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and vendor drawings are frozen ahead of foundation design; the client free-issues no equipment; a single mobilisation; utilities (grid power, water, gas/steam where applicable) are available to the site boundary by the date assumed. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy lifts (presses, mills, cranes) require crane windows and clear laydown; production-floor works need protection from later trades' traffic. Skilled commissioning and machine-vendor technicians are shared across lines and are a resource constraint late in the programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-lead equipment or steel slippage, foundation rework once a vendor's final loading data arrives, and line-integration re-test loops. Schedule contingency is held before line integration and before the loaded ramp-up rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
